hard.simple_explanation: The basic physical and organizational structures (e.g., buildings, roads, power supplies) needed for the operation of a society.
hard.funny_explanation: The skeleton of a city; if it breaks, everything turns into a messy puddle of traffic and darkness.

examples.text: The city invested in new infrastructure to support the growing population.
My personal infrastructure is held together by three coffee cups and a prayer.

hard.real_world_analogy: The plumbing and wiring inside your house that you never see until the lights go out or the sink leaks.

words.meaning: Supplying water to crops.

medium.simple_explanation: A system of supplying water to land or crops to help them grow.
medium.funny_explanation: Basically a giant, complicated shower for plants who are tired of waiting for rain.

examples.text: The farmer built a canal for irrigation during the dry summer months.
My attempt at lawn irrigation ended up watering the neighbor's cat instead.

words.meaning: Health and happiness of a group.
A suggestion for the best course of action.

medium.simple_explanation: A suggestion or advice about what someone should do.
medium.funny_explanation: A fancy way of saying 'I think you should do this, but don't blame me if it goes wrong.'

examples.text: The doctor's recommendation was to eat more fruit and exercise.
Despite my recommendation to go to bed, my cat decided to run laps at 3 AM.

words.meaning: To control something with rules.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to the process of controlling or supervising the stock exchange through rules.
hard.simple_explanation: To control or maintain the rate or speed of a machine or process so that it operates properly.
hard.funny_explanation: Being the hall monitor of the world, making sure nobody runs or creates chaos.

examples.text: New laws were passed to regulate the use of plastic in the city.
I try to regulate my screen time, but my thumb has a mind of its own.

hard.real_world_analogy: A thermostat in an AC that keeps the room from getting too hot or too cold.

words.meaning: Giving one thing and receiving another.
A strong disagreement or argument.

medium.simple_explanation: A disagreement, argument, or debate between two parties.
medium.funny_explanation: A high-stakes 'he-said, she-said' that usually ends up with a judge or a teacher getting involved.

examples.text: The court was asked to settle a land dispute between the two neighbors.
There was a heated dispute over whether a hotdog is technically a sandwich.

words.meaning: Puts a plan or decision into action.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Describes the action of putting government decisions into effect.
hard.simple_explanation: To put a decision, plan, or agreement into effect.
hard.funny_explanation: The moment you stop talking about cleaning your room and actually pick up the first sock.

examples.text: The local council implements new recycling rules starting next month.
I have a great plan to be a billionaire; I just haven't found a way to implement the 'earning money' part.

hard.real_world_analogy: A chef cooking the food after the waiter has taken the order.

words.meaning: Help for people in a bad situation.
People harmed or killed in an event.
Right or suitable for the situation.

medium.simple_explanation: Something that is suitable, right, or correct for a certain situation.
medium.funny_explanation: Wearing pajamas to bed is appropriate; wearing them to meet the Prime Minister is... a bold choice.

examples.text: Please choose the most appropriate word to complete the sentence.
Laughing during a movie is appropriate, unless it's a very sad scene about a lost puppy.

words.meaning: Government where people vote for leaders.
More than half of a group.
The end of a fixed period of time.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Relates to the end of a Prime Minister's or government's fixed term in office.
hard.simple_explanation: The end of the period for which something is valid or exists.
hard.funny_explanation: The 'game over' screen for things like milk, medicine, and political terms.

examples.text: The contract was renewed just before its expiry.
My patience with this slow internet has reached its expiry date.

hard.real_world_analogy: The final buzzer at the end of a football match.

words.meaning: Chosen officially for a job.
The total amount of money spent.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to the large amount of money spent on conducting elections.
hard.simple_explanation: The act of spending money, or the amount of money spent.
hard.funny_explanation: The magic trick where your money disappears and turns into things you probably didn't need.

examples.text: The government needs to reduce its annual expenditure to balance the budget.
My monthly expenditure on pizza is higher than my expenditure on books.

hard.real_world_analogy: Water flowing out of a tap; the faster you open it, the more you spend.

words.meaning: Large organizations that help society function.

medium.simple_explanation: Established organizations or systems that help a country run, like the government, courts, or banks.
medium.funny_explanation: Think of them as the 'Rules of the Game' for grown-ups, but with big buildings and lots of paperwork.

examples.text: The rule of law is maintained through various political institutions.
The school cafeteria is a hungry student's favorite institution, especially on Pizza Friday.

words.meaning: Likely to cause harm or trouble.
An idea that is not based on reality.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Used to describe Shankar's view that a single minister changing everything in one day is unrealistic.
hard.simple_explanation: An idea or situation that is imagined and very unlikely to happen in real life.
hard.funny_explanation: The magical belief that you will actually start studying the moment you sit down with your books instead of scrolling on your phone.

examples.text: The idea of a world without any rules is a complete fantasy.
Living in a house made of chocolate is a delicious but sticky fantasy.

hard.real_world_analogy: A daydream where you suddenly gain superpowers and fly to school.

words.meaning: High government official in charge of a department.
A feeling or action in response to something.
Groups of people who make laws for a country.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to one of the three main organs of government responsible for making laws.
hard.simple_explanation: Groups of people who have the legal power to make, change, or remove laws.
hard.funny_explanation: The ultimate debating club where adults argue for hours just to decide what the new rules of the country should be.

examples.text: The legislatures are responsible for debating and passing new bills.
If our class had a legislature, we would probably pass a law making every Friday a 'No Homework' day.

hard.real_world_analogy: The school management committee that decides the school's rules and curriculum.

words.meaning: Relating to the government or public affairs.
The part of government that carries out laws.

medium.simple_explanation: The branch of government responsible for implementing laws and making sure things get done.
medium.funny_explanation: The 'Doers' who have to actually carry out the plans while everyone else is still busy arguing about them.

examples.text: The political executive includes the Prime Minister and the Cabinet.
In our house, Mom is the executive who decides if we actually follow the 'no video games before homework' law.

words.meaning: The branch of government that handles legal courts.

medium.simple_explanation: The system of courts and judges that interprets the law and settles legal disputes.
medium.funny_explanation: The ultimate referees of the country who can blow the whistle on anyone, even the leaders.

examples.text: An independent judiciary is essential for a healthy democracy.
When we fight over the TV remote, Grandpa acts as the judiciary and makes a final ruling.

words.meaning: Things done to get ready for an event.

medium.simple_explanation: The process of getting ready for an event or activity.
medium.funny_explanation: All the frantic cleaning you do five minutes before your friends arrive for a party.

examples.text: The teacher made careful preparations for the mock parliament session.
My preparations for the exam mostly involved sharpening seventeen pencils and staring at the clock.

words.meaning: Not real but done for practice.

medium.simple_explanation: Something that is not real but is done to practice or show how something works.
medium.funny_explanation: It's like playing a video game version of real life—all the action, but nobody actually goes to jail.

examples.text: The students enjoyed participating in a mock election to learn how voting works.
I gave a mock speech to my teddy bears to practice for the school talent show.

words.meaning: National group of people who make laws.

medium.simple_explanation: A group of elected representatives who meet to discuss and create the laws of a country.
medium.funny_explanation: A very fancy room where a lot of people in suits talk for hours and hours to decide what we can and can't do.

examples.text: The law was debated extensively in Parliament before being passed.
If my family were a parliament, we would spend three hours debating whether pineapple belongs on pizza.

words.meaning: People who guide or control a group.
One of several choices you can make.
More than half of the people in a group.

medium.simple_explanation: A number or amount that is more than half of a total group.
medium.funny_explanation: The power of having one more person on your side than the other guys have.

examples.text: To pass the bill, the party needed a majority in the Lok Sabha.
The majority of the class voted for extra recess, but the teacher was the 'supreme court' and said no.

words.meaning: Saving a place or position for specific groups.

medium.simple_explanation: Keeping seats or positions specifically for certain groups of people to ensure fairness.
medium.funny_explanation: Like putting a 'Saved' sign on a chair so your best friend doesn't have to sit on the floor.

examples.text: The government issued a reservation order for backward classes in services.
I tried to make a reservation for the best spot on the couch, but the cat got there first.

words.meaning: A command given by someone in authority.
The part someone plays in a situation.
Free from outside control or influence.

medium.simple_explanation: Not being controlled or influenced by others; free to make your own choices.
medium.funny_explanation: Being the boss of your own brain and not having to ask permission to think.

examples.text: Judges must be independent so they can make fair decisions without political pressure.
I became independent the day I learned how to tie my own shoelaces... and then I tripped.

words.meaning: A final decision made by a court.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Refers to the formal decision given by the Supreme Court regarding a government order.
hard.simple_explanation: An official decision made by a jury or a court of law.
hard.funny_explanation: The final 'Yes' or 'No' your parents give after you’ve spent three days begging for a new video game.

examples.text: The public waited eagerly for the court's verdict on the controversial case.
The jury's verdict was unanimous: the cat was definitely the one who broke the flower pot.

hard.real_world_analogy: The referee's final signal that confirms whether a goal was scored or not.

words.meaning: To change something slightly to improve it.

medium.simple_explanation: To make small changes to something to improve it or make it more acceptable.
medium.funny_explanation: Tweaking your homework answers after you realize you forgot to carry the one.

examples.text: The court directed the government to modify the original order.
I had to modify my 'world's best athlete' claim after I lost a race to a toddler.

words.meaning: Someone who follows established rules and customs.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Used to describe a person or institution that simply follows established rules or patterns without questioning.
hard.simple_explanation: Someone who behaves or thinks like everyone else, following accepted rules or customs.
hard.funny_explanation: The student who wears a perfectly ironed uniform and polished shoes even on a 'color dress' day just to follow the vibe of a school.

examples.text: She was not a conformist and often challenged the old ways of doing things.
A conformist penguin would never try to fly, even if all the other birds were doing it.

hard.real_world_analogy: A person who always orders the most popular dish at a restaurant because 'everyone else likes it'.

words.meaning: Person who helps solve a disagreement between others.

hard.why_it_is_given_in_book: Describes the judiciary's role in resolving conflicts between opposing groups.
hard.simple_explanation: A person or group that helps two people or parties in a dispute to come to an agreement.
hard.funny_explanation: The brave friend who stands between two people fighting over the last slice of pizza to help them split it fairly.

examples.text: The teacher acted as a mediator to resolve the argument between the two students.
My dog is a great mediator; whenever we argue, he just barks until we stop and pet him.

hard.real_world_analogy: The referee on a sports field who ensures both teams follow the rules and settles disputes.

words.meaning: Being completely different or against another side.

medium.simple_explanation: Being against something or representing the other side of an argument.
medium.funny_explanation: Like the 'Broccoli Lovers' versus the 'Broccoli Haters'—they just can't agree on dinner.

examples.text: The mediator helped find a balance between the two opposing parties.
My cat and my dog have opposing views on who owns the sunspot on the rug.

words.meaning: State where different parts are treated equally.
Printed sheets containing daily news and information.
To put things into groups based on features.

medium.simple_explanation: To arrange things into groups based on how they are similar.
medium.funny_explanation: Sorting your laundry into 'smells okay' and 'needs a hazmat suit.'

examples.text: Students were asked to classify news reports into four different groups.
I classify my snacks into 'healthy stuff I should eat' and 'delicious stuff I already ate.'
